messages.body_plain:
Hi,

it depends what you mean by issues. Technically you can do it. What is more relevant is the assumptions that are implied, most importantly the closure assumption. It will not hold over many years.

Also, using multi-sessions allows you to estimate additional parameters (extinction and colonization probabilities) and how they are affected by covariates.

The best choice depends on the study design and how it relates to the assumptions of the models.

See the colext vignette in unmarked for some thorough explanations and examples.

Cheers,

Jürgen

messages.subject: Re: [camtrapR] Are detectionMaps adjusted for effort?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michelle,

I suppose you mean detection rates, e.g. XY detections per 100 trap nights? The detectionMaps function does currently not take that into account. Maybe in the future (someone offer to improve the rather basic plotting functions), but for time being there is no readymade solution and you'd probably have to do some data wrangling yourself. The output of cameraOperation or surveyReport give you the effory by station, which can be used to calculate detection rates. Then you can easily plot that with base R or ggplot.

It was an intentional omission though, because detection rates don't account for detection probabilities and can thus be misleading.

Apart from that I'm happy to hear you enjoy the package.

Best regards,

Jürgen

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabby,
for whatever reason these photos seem to have no dateTimeOriginal tag. In fact there are not Exif metadata at all, which is unfortunate.
Is the FileModifyDate  (2009-07-05 ...) correct? Or the date under "Comment" (line 18)?
If yes, exiftool can copy image tags, and that way you could potentially create a DateTimeOriginal tag. Since it is quite a special case there is no camtrapR function for this (yet).

You can also try installing the dev version of camtrapR, it contains a new function OCRdataFields which allows you to read the date/time and whatever else from the data fields in the images.  It is not always  100% correct, so check the output carefully. It requires the magick and tesseract packages.
But please note, it is work in progress and currently only gives you a data frame with the extracted tags, and doesn't write the tags into the images. So the normal recordTable operation still won't work since it expects the DateTimeOriginal tag.

library(devtools)
install_github("jniedballa/camtrapR", ref = "dev")

Best regards,
Jürgen

Hi David,
that's an interesting idea, but I am not sure it is really needed. Like you said, one can achieve that with a for loop, or maybe even better, lapply(). That would at least save you the manual copying.
detectionMaps will automatically plot all species, unless you specify the parameter "speciesToShow". For detectionHistory, you can use lapply like this:

data(camtraps)
data(recordTableSample)

camop_no_problem <- cameraOperation(CTtable      = camtraps,
                                    stationCol   = "Station",
                                    setupCol     = "Setup_date",
                                    retrievalCol = "Retrieval_date",
                                    hasProblems  = FALSE,
                                    dateFormat   = "%d/%m/%Y"
)

species <- c("PBE", "VTA")

list_dh <- lapply(species, FUN = detectionHistory,
                  recordTable     = recordTableSample,
                  camOp           = camop_no_problem,
                  occasionLength  = 7,
                  day1            = "station",
                  includeEffort   = TRUE,
                  scaleEffort     = FALSE
)
names(list_dh) <- species

> list_dh
$PBE

Hi Gabby,
I just added a function to the development  version of the package that allows you to write new values to the DateTimeOriginal field in the exif metadata of images (or create a new DateTimeOriginal field if it is missing). So you can first run OCRdataFields to extract the date/time values from the data fields in the images as mentioned before, check them (that's important because OCR can make mistakes), and then run the new function writeDateTimeOriginal to create a new DateTimeOriginal field.
To use it, please reinstall the dev version and see the "Examples" section in the function documentation on how to use it in conjunction with OCRdataFields.

If you give it a try, please let me know how it goes. I just wrote the function and didn't test it on a larger data set yet, so all feedback would be valuable.
Best,
Jürgen

messages.body_plain:
Hi Katie,
the main problem with treating multiple seasons as one season (one row per camera and using the problem columns) is the closure assumption, which will most likely not hold over extended time frames.
So yes, I believe using the session column would be the best way forward. In your case it would mean separating the multiple deployments into separate rows and creating a session column to keep them apart.

camtrapR contains sample data and sample code for multi-season analyses which you can use as guidance. Please see the vignette for some more explanations and examples for multi-season occupancy models:
https://jniedballa.github.io/camtrapR/articles/camtrapr3.html#multi-season-occupancy-analyses

?camtrapsMultiSeason
?recordTableSampleMultiSeason

The examples of detectionHistory() show how to use them to create unmarkedFrames.
Best,
Jürgen

Hi Dipankar,
and sorry for the late reply. I think the easiest would be to combine the grid and station name into a unique station ID. In your example above, the station could be: "625_Barbala-River". Then you can have your cameras (A) and date/time in the file names as usual.

Please also note that in imageRename, the station, camera, date and time are separated with double underscores. So if you separate grid and station with a single underscore (for example) you can separate them later if necessary.

 It is a bit hacky,  but I hope it will work for you. That way it should be compatible with the rest of the camtrapR workflow. I'm sorry, but I can't just easily change the renaming function without lots of unexpected consequences down the road.
Best,
Jürgen
